title: Ruckaroo
tagline: A rucking app that turns walking with weight into a scored, social workout.
summary: A fitness app for rucking (walking with weight on your back) with a Ruck Score, badges, an AI coach, stats and a community.
overview: Ruckaroo is a mobile app for rucking: walking, hiking or training with weight on your back. It calculates a Ruck Score from your pack weight, distance, terrain and body data, rewards every ruck with a badge, and connects to Apple Watch. I designed the whole app experience, from the first-time onboarding and sign-up to the personal plan, plus the App Store screenshots that sell it.
problem: Most people have never heard of rucking, and most fitness apps only count steps. How might we explain a new kind of workout in a few screens, collect the personal data the Ruck Score needs, and still get people to their plan without losing them on the way?

product: Shaping the onboarding story: what rucking is, why it beats walking, what makes the app different
Deciding which personal data to ask for and in what order
Defining every state: empty, filled, error, loading and dialogs
design: General onboarding and education screens
Sign up, login, forgot password and confirmation code flows
Personal onboarding: name, @handle, birthday, gender, weight, height, goal and challenge
Plan building, notifications and review prompts
App Store screenshots
Illustrations and visual style

process.title: Understand the sport
process.desc: Learned how rucking works and what the Ruck Score is built on (pack weight, distance and pace, terrain, body weight, heart rate, temperature and humidity) so the screens explain it in plain words.

process.title: Tell the story first
process.desc: Opened with short education screens: what rucking is, walking versus rucking, the badges and the wearable, before asking the user for anything.

process.title: Collect data step by step
process.desc: One question per screen with a progress bar, unit toggles (lbs/kg, ft-in/cm), pickers instead of typing, and a clear empty state for every step.

process.title: Design every state
process.desc: Default, typing, filled and error states for every form, plus loading, cancel dialogs and success screens.

process.title: Sell it in the store
process.desc: Designed a set of App Store screenshots that each carry one benefit: calories, science, Ruck Score, coach, stats, sharing and syncing.

challenges.challenge: Rucking is new to most users, so the value is not obvious.
challenges.solution: Education screens with a simple comparison (walking vs rucking) and a five-level badge system before any sign-up friction.

challenges.challenge: The Ruck Score needs a lot of personal data, which can feel like a long form.
challenges.solution: Split it into single-question screens with pickers, unit toggles and a progress bar, and explained why each answer matters.

challenges.challenge: Many form fields and edge cases across auth flows.
challenges.solution: Defined a consistent set of field states and error messages reused across sign up, login and password recovery.

learnings: Designing for a sport most people do not know yet taught me to lead with the story before the form. I practised building a long onboarding that still feels light, designing every form state carefully, and turning product benefits into a set of App Store screenshots.

title: Mazadak
tagline: An auction app where you bid with points, not cash.
summary: A mobile auction app where people earn points from local merchants and spend them on bids. The highest unique bid wins, so luck and strategy both matter.
overview: Mazadak (Arabic for “your auction”) turns shopping into a game. Customers scan a merchant’s QR code to collect points, then use those points to bid on products. Each bid costs points, every user gets a limited number of bids, and the highest unique bid wins when the auction ends. I designed the product end to end: onboarding, sign-up and login, the auction flow with every state, merchants, QR scanning, history and profile, in Arabic and English.
problem: Auctions usually reward whoever has the most money. How might we make them fair and fun, and give local merchants a reason for customers to come back?

challenges.challenge: “Highest unique bid wins” is new to most people.
challenges.solution: Onboarding explains it in three steps, the rules sit right above the bid input, and a comparison sheet shows which bids matched yours.

challenges.challenge: An auction changes a lot over its life.
challenges.solution: One details screen with clear status tags (Active, Extended, Failed, Ended), a progress bar toward the bid target and a live countdown.

challenges.challenge: Users must always know what they can still do.
challenges.solution: Points balance and bid progress (1/5) next to the bid button, with warnings when bids or points run out.

learnings: Mazadak was a chance to discover more design skills on a product with real rules behind it: designing a points economy, explaining an unusual mechanic simply, and handling every state an auction can be in. It also taught me how much small moments, like a level-up or a “Cha-Ching!”, make a product feel alive.
